claims.evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the findings presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Perception goes beyond the immediate sensory evidence and draws heavily on context and prior experience.
claims.source: In deducing the likely physical causes of sensations, perception goes beyond the immediate sensory evidence and draws heavily on context and prior experience (von Helmholtz, 1867; Barlow et al., 1972; Gregory, 1980; Rock, 1983).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to classical work in perception.

claims.claim: Numerous illusions in visual, auditory, and tactile perception attest to perception's extrapolation beyond the evidence.
claims.source: Numerous illusions in visual, auditory, and tactile perception – all subjectively compelling, but objectively false – attest to this extrapolation beyond the evidence.
claims.evidence: This is based on well-established knowledge about perceptual illusions.

claims.claim: In natural settings, perception explores alternative plausible causes of sensory evidence by active readjustment of sensors.
claims.source: In natural settings, perception explores alternative plausible causes of sensory evidence by active readjustment of sensors ('active perception,' Mirza et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2018; Parr and Friston, 2017a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to recent work on active perception.

claims.claim: Perception is thought to actively select plausible explanatory hypotheses, to predict the sensory evidence expected for each hypothesis from prior experience, and to compare the observed sensory evidence at multiple levels of scale or abstraction.
claims.source: In general, perception is thought to actively select plausible explanatory hypotheses, to predict the sensory evidence expected for each hypothesis from prior experience, and to compare the observed sensory evidence at multiple levels of scale or abstraction ('analysis by synthesis,' 'predictive coding,' 'hierarchical Bayesian inference,' Yuille and Kersten, 2006, Rao and Ballard, 1999, Parr and Friston, 2017b, Pezzulo et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical frameworks in perception.

claims.claim: Active inference engages the entire hierarchy of cortical areas involved in sensory processing, including both feedforward and feedback projections.
claims.source: Active inference engages the entire hierarchy of cortical areas involved in sensory processing, including both feedforward and feedback projections (Bar, 2009; Larkum, 2013; Shipp, 2016; Funamizu et al., 2016; Parr et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to neuroscience literature.

claims.claim: The dynamics of active inference becomes experimentally observable when perceptual illusions are 'multistable'.
claims.source: The dynamics of active inference becomes experimentally observable when perceptual illusions are 'multistable' (Leopold and Logothetis, 1999).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to work on multistable perception.

claims.claim: In numerous ambiguous or conflicting situations, phenomenal experience switches at irregular intervals between discrete alternatives, even though the sensory scene is stable.
claims.source: In numerous ambiguous or conflicting situations, phenomenal experience switches at irregular intervals between discrete alternatives, even though the sensory scene is stable (Necker, 2009; Wheatstone, 1838; Rubin, 1958; Attneave, 1971; Ramachandran and Anstis, 2016; Pressnitzer and Hupe, 2006; Schwartz et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to classic and recent work on multistable perception.

claims.claim: Multistable illusions are enormously diverse, involving visibility or audibility, perceptual grouping, visual depth or motion, and many kinds of sensory scenes, from schematic to naturalistic.
claims.source: Multistable illusions are enormously diverse, involving visibility or audibility, perceptual grouping, visual depth or motion, and many kinds of sensory scenes, from schematic to naturalistic.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the variety of multistable phenomena.

claims.claim: Average switching rates differ greatly and range over at least two orders of magnitude, depending on sensory scene, perceptual grouping, continuous or intermittent presentation, attentional condition, individual observer, and many other factors.
claims.source: Average switching rates differ greatly and range over at least two orders of magnitude (Cao et al., 2016), depending on sensory scene, perceptual grouping (Wertheimer, 1912; Koffka, 1935; Ternus, 1926), continuous or intermittent presentation (Leopold and Logothetis, 2002; Maier et al., 2003), attentional condition (Pastukhov and Braun, 2007), individual observer (Pastukhov et al., 2013c; Denham et al., 2018; Brascamp et al., 2019), and many other factors.
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claims.claim: The stochastic properties of multistable phenomena appear to be quasi-universal, suggesting that the underlying mechanisms may be general.
claims.source: In spite of this diversity, the stochastic properties of multistable phenomena appear to be quasi-universal, suggesting that the underlying mechanisms may be general.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of similar statistical patterns across diverse phenomena.

claims.claim: Average dominance duration depends in a characteristic and counterintuitive manner on the strength of dominant and suppressed evidence ('Levelt's propositions I–IV').
claims.source: Firstly, average dominance duration depends in a characteristic and counterintuitive manner on the strength of dominant and suppressed evidence ('Levelt's propositions I–IV,' Levelt, 1965; Brascamp et al., 2006; Klink et al., 2016; Kang, 2009; Brascamp et al., 2015; Moreno-Bote et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies of binocular rivalry.

claims.claim: The durations of successive dominance periods are correlated positively, over at least two or three periods.
claims.source: Thirdly, the durations of successive dominance periods are correlated positively, over at least two or three periods (Fox and Herrmann, 1967; Walker, 1975; Van Ee, 2005; Denham et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claims.claim: These quasi-universal characteristics are comprehensively and quantitatively reproduced by an interacting hierarchy of birth-death processes operating out of equilibrium.
claims.source: Here, we show that these quasi-universal characteristics are comprehensively and quantitatively reproduced, indeed guaranteed, by an interacting hierarchy of birth-death processes operating out of equilibrium.
claims.evidence: This is the main claim of the manuscript, supported by model simulations and experimental comparisons.

claims.claim: The proposed mechanism combines some of the key features of previous models, but far surpasses their explanatory power.
claims.source: While the proposed mechanism combines some of the key features of previous models, it far surpasses their explanatory power.
claims.evidence: This is argued based on the comprehensive reproduction of experimental observations.

claims.claim: A single, coherent interpretation typically dominates phenomenal experience, which is thought to reflect competition at the level of explanatory hypotheses, sensory inputs, or both.
claims.source: That a single, coherent interpretation typically dominates phenomenal experience is thought to reflect competition (explicit or implicit) at the level of explanatory hypotheses (e.g., Dayan, 1998), sensory inputs (e.g., Lehky, 1988), or both (e.g., Wilson, 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical models.

claims.claim: A dominant interpretation is occasionally supplanted by a distinct alternative, which has been attributed to fatigue processes, spontaneous fluctuations, stochastic sampling, or combinations of these.
claims.source: That a dominant interpretation is occasionally supplanted by a distinct alternative has been attributed to fatigue processes (e.g., neural adaptation, synaptic depression, Laing and Chow, 2002), spontaneous fluctuations ('noise,' e.g., Wilson, 2007, Kim et al., 2006), stochastic sampling (e.g., Schrater and Sundareswara, 2006), or combinations of these (e.g., adaptation and noise, Shpiro et al., 2009; Seely and Chow, 2011; Pastukhov et al., 2013c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to various theoretical models.

claims.claim: The characteristic stochasticity of dominance durations has been attributed to Poisson counting processes or stochastic accumulation of discrete samples.
claims.source: The characteristic stochasticity (gamma-like distribution) of dominance durations has been attributed to Poisson counting processes (e.g., birth-death processes, Taylor and Ladridge, 1974; Gigante et al., 2009; Cao et al., 2016) or stochastic accumulation of discrete samples (Murata et al., 2003; Schrater and Sundareswara, 2006; Sundareswara and Schrater, 2008; Weilnhammer et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical models.

claims.claim: 'Dynamical' models combining competition, adaptation, and noise capture well the characteristic dependence of dominance durations on input strength ('Levelt's propositions').
claims.source: 'Dynamical' models combining competition, adaptation, and noise capture well the characteristic dependence of dominance durations on input strength ('Levelt's propositions') (Laing and Chow, 2002; Wilson, 2007; Ashwin and Aureliu, 2010), especially when inputs are normalized (Moreno-Bote et al., 2007; Moreno-Bote et al., 2010; Cohen et al., 2019), and when the dynamics emphasize noise (Shpiro et al., 2009; Seely and Chow, 2011; Pastukhov et al., 2013c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous modeling work.

claims.claim: Dynamical models do not preserve distribution shape over the full range of input strengths.
claims.source: However, such models do not preserve distribution shape over the full range of input strengths (Cao et al., 2016; Cohen et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies evaluating previous models.

claims.claim: 'Sampling' models based on discrete random processes preserve distribution shape but fail to reproduce the dependence on input strength.
claims.source: On the other hand, 'sampling' models based on discrete random processes preserve distribution shape (Taylor and Ladridge, 1974; Murata et al., 2003; Schrater and Sundareswara, 2006; Sundareswara and Schrater, 2008; Cao et al., 2016; Weilnhammer et al., 2017), but fail to reproduce the dependence on input strength.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous modeling work.

claims.claim: Neither 'dynamical' nor 'sampling' models account for the sequential dependence of dominance durations.
claims.source: Neither type of model accounts for the sequential dependence of dominance durations (Laing and Chow, 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous model.

claims.claim: The proposed mechanism reconciles 'dynamical' and 'sampling' approaches to multistable perception.
claims.source: Here, we reconcile 'dynamical' and 'sampling' approaches to multistable perception, extending an earlier effort (Gigante et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the contribution of the present work, supported by the model description and results.

claims.claim: Every part of the proposed mechanism appears to be justified normatively in that it may serve to optimize perceptual choices in continuous inference in uncertain and volatile environments.
claims.source: Importantly, every part of the proposed mechanism appears to be justified normatively in that it may serve to optimize perceptual choices in a general behavioral situation, namely, continuous inference in uncertain and volatile environments (Bogacz, 2007; Veliz-Cuba et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is argued theoretically with citations to work on optimal decision-making.

claims.claim: Sensory inputs are represented by birth-death processes in order to accumulate sensory information over time and in a format suited for Bayesian inference.
claims.source: We propose that sensory inputs are represented by birth-death processes in order to accumulate sensory information over time and in a format suited for Bayesian inference (Ma et al., 2006; Pouget et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical proposal supported by citations to work on neural coding.

claims.claim: Explanatory hypotheses are evaluated competitively, with a hypothesis attaining dominance when its support exceeds the alternatives by a certain finite amount, consistent with optimal decision-making between multiple alternatives.
claims.source: Further, we suggest that explanatory hypotheses are evaluated competitively, with a hypothesis attaining dominance (over phenomenal experience) when its support exceeds the alternatives by a certain finite amount, consistent with optimal decision-making between multiple alternatives (Bogacz, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical proposal supported by a citation to work on optimal decision-making.

claims.claim: A dominant hypothesis suppresses its supporting evidence, as required by 'predictive coding' implementations of hierarchical Bayesian inference.
claims.source: Finally, we assume that a dominant hypothesis suppresses its supporting evidence, as required by 'predictive coding' implementations of hierarchical Bayesian inference (Pearl, 1988; Rao and Ballard, 1999; Hohwy et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical proposal supported by citations to work on predictive coding.

claims.claim: The proposed mechanism does not require a local mechanism of fatigue, adaptation, or decay.
claims.source: In contrast to many previous models, we do not require a local mechanisms of fatigue, adaptation, or decay.
claims.evidence: This is a description of how the proposed model differs from previous models.

claims.claim: The proposed mechanism reproduces dependence on input strength, distribution of dominance durations, and positive sequential dependence.
claims.source: Based on these assumptions, the proposed mechanism reproduces dependence on input strength, as well as distribution of dominance durations and positive sequential dependence.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the model simulations and experimental comparisons presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The mechanism predicts novel and unsuspected dynamical features confirmed by experiment.
claims.source: Additionally, it predicts novel and unsuspected dynamical features confirmed by experiment.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the experimental observations of previously unreported features.

claims.claim: Binocular rivalry arises when the left and right eyes see incompatible images in the visual field, causing phenomenal appearance to reverse at irregular intervals.
claims.source: When the left and right eyes see incompatible images in the visual field, phenomenal appearance reverses at irregular intervals, sometimes being dominated by one image and sometimes by the other (gray and white regions).
claims.evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1a and is a well-known phenomenon.

claims.claim: A spiking neural network implementation of a 'local attractor' shows an assembly of 150 neurons that interacts competitively with multiple other assemblies.
claims.source: Spiking neural network implementation of a 'local attractor.' An assembly of 150 neurons (schematic, dark gray circle) interacts competitively with multiple other assemblies (light gray circles).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1b and described in the text.

claims.claim: Population activity of the assembly explores an effective energy landscape with two distinct steady states, separated by a ridge.
claims.source: Population activity of the assembly explores an effective energy landscape (right) with two distinct steady states (circles), separated by a ridge (diamond).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1b and described in the text.

claims.claim: The nested attractor dynamics quantitatively reproduces the dynamics of binocular rivalry.
claims.source: Nested attractor dynamics (central schematic) that quantitatively reproduces the dynamics of binocular rivalry (left and right columns).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1c and described in the text.

claims.claim: Independently bistable variables respond probabilistically to input, transitioning stochastically between on- and off-states.
claims.source: Independently bistable variables ('local attractors,' small circles) respond probabilistically to input, transitioning stochastically between on- and off-states (red/blue and white, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1c and described in the text.

claims.claim: The entire system comprises four pools, with 25 variables each, linked by excitatory and inhibitory projections.
claims.source: The entire system comprises four pools, with 25 variables each, linked by excitatory and inhibitory projections.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1c and described in the text.

claims.claim: In decision pools, almost all variables become active or inactive simultaneously.
claims.source: In decision pools, almost all variables become active (black trace) or inactive (no trace) simultaneously.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1c and described in the text.

claims.claim: In evidence pools, only a small fraction of variables is active at any given time.
claims.source: In evidence pools, only a small fraction of variables is active at any given time.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1c and described in the text.

claims.claim: Neuronal assemblies with bistable 'attractor' dynamics are postulated as operative units of sensory representation.
claims.source: As operative units of sensory representation, we postulate neuronal assemblies with bistable 'attractor' dynamics.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical proposal that forms the basis of the model.

claims.claim: Assembly activity moves in an energy landscape with two distinct quasi-stable states – dubbed 'on' and 'off' – separated by a ridge.
claims.source: Effectively, assembly activity moves in an energy landscape with two distinct quasi-stable states – dubbed 'on' and 'off' – separated by a ridge (Figure 1b).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1b and described in the text.

claims.claim: Driven by noise, assembly activity mostly remains near one quasi-stable state, but occasionally 'escapes' to the other state.
claims.source: Driven by noise, assembly activity mostly remains near one quasi-stable state ('on' or 'off'), but occasionally 'escapes' to the other state (Kramers, 1940; Hanggi et al., 1990; Deco and Hugues, 2012; Litwin-Kumar and Doiron, 2012; Huang and Doiron, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work on noise-driven transitions.

claims.claim: The energy of quasi-stable states depends sensitively on external input.
claims.source: An important feature of 'attractor' dynamics is that the energy of quasi-stable states depends sensitively on external input.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical property of attractor dynamics.

claims.claim: Net positive input destabilizes the 'off' state and stabilizes the 'on' state.
claims.source: Net positive input destabilizes (i.e., raises the potential of) the 'off' state and stabilizes (i.e., lowers the potential of) the 'on' state.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical property of attractor dynamics.

claims.claim: The model is independent of neural details and relies exclusively on an idealized description of 'attractor' dynamics.
claims.source: Our model is independent of neural details and relies exclusively on an idealized description of 'attractor' dynamics.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the modeling approach.

claims.claim: Pools of bistable variables belong to a class of neural representations particularly suited for Bayesian integration of sensory information.
claims.source: Pools of bistable variables belong to a class of neural representations particularly suited for Bayesian integration of sensory information (Beck et al., 2008; Pouget et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to work on neural coding.

claims.claim: Summation of activity is equivalent to optimal integration of information, provided that response variability is Poisson-like, and response tuning differs only multiplicatively.
claims.source: In general, summation of activity is equivalent to optimal integration of information, provided that response variability is Poisson-like, and response tuning differs only multiplicatively (Ma et al., 2006; Ma et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to work on neural coding.

claims.claim: Pools of bistable variables closely approximate the properties required for optimal integration of information.
claims.source: Pools of bistable variables closely approximate these properties (see Appendix 1, section Quality of representation: Suitability for inference).
claims.evidence: This is argued in the Appendix.

claims.claim: A winner-take-all decision is readily accomplished by a dynamical version of biased competition.
claims.source: Such a winner-take-all decision (Koch and Ullman, 1985) is readily accomplished by a dynamical version of biased competition (Deco and Rolls, 2005; Wang, 2002; Deco et al., 2007; Wang, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous modeling work.

claims.claim: Recurrent excitation within pools and recurrent inhibition between pools obtain a 'winner-take-all' dynamics.
claims.source: Similar to previous models of decision-making and attentional selection (Deco and Rolls, 2005; Wang, 2002; Deco et al., 2007; Wang, 2008), we postulate recurrent excitation within pools, but recurrent inhibition between pools, to obtain a 'winner-take-all' dynamics.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous modeling work.

claims.claim: 'Evidence pools' project to 'decision pools' in the form of selective excitation and indiscriminate inhibition.
claims.source: Importantly, we assume that 'evidence pools' project to 'decision pools' not only in the form of selective excitation (targeted at the corresponding decision pool), but also in the form of indiscriminate inhibition (targeting both decision pools), as suggested previously (Ditterich et al., 2003; Bogacz et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous modeling work.

claims.claim: Each decision pool selectively targets the corresponding evidence pool with feedback suppression.
claims.source: Finally, we assume feedback suppression, with each decision pool selectively targeting the corresponding evidence pool.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model architecture.

claims.claim: Effects of feedback suppression include curtailment of dominance durations and ensuring that reversals occur from time to time.
claims.source: Its effects include curtailment of dominance durations and ensuring that reversals occur from time to time.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model dynamics.

claims.claim: Previous models have justified selective feedback suppression in terms of 'predictive coding' and 'hierarchical Bayesian inference'.
claims.source: Previous models of BR (Dayan, 1998; Hohwy et al., 2008) have justified selective feedback suppression of the evidence supporting a winning hypothesis in terms of 'predictive coding' and 'hierarchical Bayesian inference' (Rao and Ballard, 1999; Lee and Mumford, 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous modeling work.

claims.claim: In volatile environments, optimal inference requires an exponentially growing bias against evidence for the most likely hypothesis.
claims.source: An alternative normative justification is that, in volatile environments, where the sensory situation changes frequently ('volatility prior'), optimal inference requires an exponentially growing bias against evidence for the most likely hypothesis (Veliz-Cuba et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to work on optimal inference.

claims.claim: Feedback suppression applies selectively to evidence for a winning hypothesis and is materially different from visual adaptation.
claims.source: Note that feedback suppression applies selectively to evidence for a winning hypothesis and is thus materially different from visual adaptation (Wark et al., 2009), which applies indiscriminately to all evidence present.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical distinction with a citation.

claims.claim: As soon as the reversal has been effected at the decision level, feedback suppression lifts from the newly non-dominant evidence and descends upon the newly dominant evidence.
claims.source: As soon as the reversal has been effected at the decision level, feedback suppression lifts from the newly non-dominant evidence and descends upon the newly dominant evidence.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model dynamics.

claims.claim: Due to asymmetric suppression, the newly non-dominant evidence recovers, whereas the newly dominant evidence habituates.
claims.source: Due to this asymmetric suppression, the newly non-dominant evidence recovers, whereas the newly dominant evidence habituates.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model dynamics.

claims.claim: The activity of decision pools varies in phase (or counterphase) with perceptual appearance, while the activity of evidence pools changes in quarterphase (or negative quarterphase) with perceptual appearance.
claims.source: Whereas the activity of decision pools varies in phase (or counterphase) with perceptual appearance, the activity of evidence pools changes in quarterphase (or negative quarterphase) with perceptual appearance (e.g., Figures 1c,d,2a), consistent with some previous models (Gigante et al., 2009; Albert et al., 2017; Weilnhammer et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figures 1c,d,2a and is consistent with previous models.

claims.claim: Six practiced observers participated in the experiment.
claims.source: Six practiced observers participated in the experiment (four males, two females).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claims.claim: Informed consent, and consent to publish, was obtained from all observers.
claims.source: Informed consent, and consent to publish, was obtained from all observers, and ethical approval Z22/16 was obtained from the Ethics Commission of the Faculty of Medicine of the Otto-von-Guericke University, Magdeburg.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the ethical procedures.

claims.claim: Five contrast levels were used: 6.25, 12.5, 25, 50, and 100%.
claims.source: Five contrast levels were used: 6.25, 12.5, 25, 50, and 100%.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claims.claim: Minimization of the fit error revealed a high degree of redundancy among the 11 model parameters.
claims.source: Importantly, minimization of the fit error, by random sampling of parameter space with a stochastic gradient descent, resulted in a three-dimensional manifold of suboptimal solutions. This revealed a high degree of redundancy among the 11 model parameters (see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the fitting results.

claims.claim: The effective number of degrees of freedom needed to reproduce the desired out-of-equilibrium dynamics was between 3 and 4.
claims.source: Accordingly, we estimate that the effective number of degrees of freedom needed to reproduce the desired out-of-equilibrium dynamics was between 3 and 4.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the fitting results.

claims.claim: The complex and asymmetric dependence of mean dominance durations on image contrast is fully reproduced by the model.
claims.source: The complex and asymmetric dependence of mean dominance durations on image contrast — aptly summarized by Levelt's 'propositions' I to IV (Levelt, 1965; Brascamp et al., 2015) — is fully reproduced by the model (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 and described in the text.

claims.claim: Increasing the contrast of one image increases the fraction of time during which this image dominates appearance ('predominance,' Levelt I).
claims.source: Here, we use the updated definition of Brascamp et al., 2015: increasing the contrast of one image increases the fraction of time during which this image dominates appearance ('predominance,' Levelt I).
claims.evidence: This is a description of Levelt's proposition I with a citation.

claims.claim: Increasing predominance is due more to shortening dominance of the unchanged image than to lengthening dominance of the changed image (Levelt II).
claims.source: Counterintuitively, this is due more to shortening dominance of the unchanged image than to lengthening dominance of the changed image (Levelt II, Figure 3b, left panel).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3b and described in the text.

claims.claim: Successive dominance durations are typically correlated positively.
claims.source: Successive dominance durations are typically correlated positively (Fox and Herrmann, 1967; Walker, 1975; Pastukhov et al., 2013c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claims.claim: This dependence of correlation on contrast was not fitted but constitutes a model prediction that is confirmed by observation.
claims.source: It is important to that this dependence was not fitted. Rather, this previously unreported dependence constitutes a model prediction that is confirmed by observation.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model prediction and experimental confirmation.

claims.claim: The fitted model fully reproduces the 'scaling property'.
claims.source: The fitted model fully reproduces this 'scaling property' (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 and described in the text.

claims.claim: Both observed and fitted values of coefficient of variation increased above, or decreased below, the typical range at extreme contrast combinations.
claims.source: Unexpectedly, both observed and fitted values increased above, or decreased below, this range at extreme contrast combinations (Figure 4b, left panel).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4b and described in the text.

claims.claim: Due to feedback suppression inverting the sign of the opponent developments, dominant evidence decreases (habituates) while non-dominant evidence increases (recovers).
claims.source: As feedback suppression inverts the sign of the opponent developments, dominant evidence decreases (habituates) while non-dominant evidence increases (recovers).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model dynamics.

claims.claim: Incrementing one input speeds up recovery or slows down habituation, shortening or lengthening periods of non-dominance and dominance, respectively (Levelt I).
claims.source: It further follows that incrementing one input (and raising the corresponding asymptotic level) speeds up recovery or slows down habituation, shortening or lengthening periods of non-dominance and dominance, respectively (Levelt I).
claims.evidence: This is a description of how the model reproduces Levelt I.

claims.claim: Dominance durations depend more sensitively on non-dominant input (Levelt II) because recovery of non-dominant evidence is generally slower than habituation of dominant evidence.
claims.source: This is why dominance durations depend more sensitively on non-dominant input (Levelt II): recovery of non-dominant evidence is generally slower than habituation of dominant evidence, independently of which input is weaker or stronger.
claims.evidence: This is a description of how the model reproduces Levelt II.

claims.claim: The hyperbolic dependence is why alternation rate peaks at equidominance (Levelt III): increasing the difference between inputs always lengthens longer durations more than it shortens shorter durations, thus lowering alternation rate.
claims.source: This hyperbolic dependence is also why alternation rate peaks at equidominance (Levelt III): increasing the difference between inputs always lengthens longer durations more than it shortens shorter durations, thus lowering alternation rate.
claims.evidence: This is a description of how the model reproduces Levelt III.

claims.claim: For all combinations of image contrast, the mechanism accurately predicts the experimentally observed distributions of dominance durations.
claims.source: For all combinations of image contrast, the mechanism accurately predicts the experimentally observed distributions of dominance durations.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the model simulations and experimental comparisons.

claims.claim: The 'scaling property' is due to the Poisson-like variability of birth-death processes.
claims.source: This is owed to the stochastic activity of pools of bistable variables. Firstly, dominance distributions retain nearly the same shape, even though average durations vary more than threefold with image contrast (see also Appendix 1—figure 6a,b). This 'scaling property' is due to the Poisson-like variability of birth-death processes (see Appendix 1, section Stochastic dynamics).
claims.evidence: This is argued in the Appendix.

claims.claim: When a stochastic accumulation approaches threshold, the rates of both accumulation and dispersion of activity affect the distribution of first-passage-times.
claims.source: Generally, when a stochastic accumulation approaches threshold, the rates of both accumulation and dispersion of activity affect the distribution of first-passage-times (Cao et al., 2014; Cao et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: In the special case of Poisson-like variability, the two rates vary proportionally and preserve distribution shape.
claims.source: In the special case of Poisson-like variability, the two rates vary proportionally and preserve distribution shape (see also Appendix 1—figure 6c,d).
claims.evidence: This is argued in the Appendix.

claims.claim: In the low-threshold regime, the first-passage-times of birth-death processes are both highly variable and gamma distributed, consistent with experimental observations.
claims.source: In this low-threshold regime, the first-passage-times of birth-death processes are both highly variable and gamma distributed, consistent with experimental observations.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model properties.

claims.claim: For longer durations, stochastic development becomes noise-dominated because stronger-input evidence habituates rapidly into a regime where random fluctuations gain importance.
claims.source: The reason is that stochastic development becomes noise-dominated. For longer durations, stronger-input evidence habituates rapidly into a regime where random fluctuations gain importance (see also Appendix 1—figure 4a,b).
claims.evidence: This is argued in the Appendix.

claims.claim: The proposed mechanism predicts positive correlations between successive dominance durations, a well-known characteristic of multistable phenomena.
claims.source: The proposed mechanism predicts positive correlations between successive dominance durations, a well-known characteristic of multistable phenomena (Fox and Herrmann, 1967; Walker, 1975; Van Ee, 2005; Denham et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claims.claim: The mechanism predicts further aspects of serial dependence not reported previously.
claims.source: In addition, it predicts further aspects of serial dependence not reported previously.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the model predictions.

claims.claim: In both model and experimental observations, a long dominance period tends to be followed by another long period, and a short dominance period by another short period.
claims.source: In both model and experimental observations, a long dominance period tends to be followed by another long period, and a short dominance period by another short period (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 6 and described in the text.

claims.claim: The autocorrelation time of mean evidence fluctuations increases monotonically with image contrast and, for high contrast, spans multiple dominance periods.
claims.source: The autocorrelation time of these fluctuations increases monotonically with image contrast and, for high contrast, spans multiple dominance periods (see Appendix 1, section Characteristic times and Appendix 1—figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is argued in the Appendix.

claims.claim: Sequential correlations are predicted (and observed) to be strictly positive at all lags.
claims.source: First, sequential correlations are predicted (and observed) to be strictly positive at all lags (next period, one-after-next period, and so on) (Figure 6d).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 6d and described in the text.

claims.claim: Sequential correlations are predicted (and observed) to increase with image contrast.
claims.source: Second, due to the contrast dependence of autocorrelation time, sequential correlations are predicted (and observed) to increase with image contrast (Figure 6d).

claims.claim: Larger pools with hundreds of bistable variables do not express the observed dependence on contrast.
claims.source: Larger pools with hundreds of bistable variables do not express the observed dependence on contrast (not shown).
claims.evidence: This is a description of model simulations.

claims.claim: For high image contrast, reversal sequences are predicted (and observed) to contain extended episodes with dominance periods that are short or extended episodes with periods that are long.
claims.source: Third, for high image contrast, reversal sequences are predicted (and observed) to contain extended episodes with dominance periods that are short or extended episodes with periods that are long (Figure 6c).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 6c and described in the text.

claims.claim: When quantified in terms of a 'burstiness index,' the degree of inhomogeneity in predicted and observed reversal sequences is comparable.
claims.source: When quantified in terms of a 'burstiness index,' the degree of inhomogeneity in predicted and observed reversal sequences is comparable (see Appendix 1, section Burstiness and Appendix 1—figure 8).
claims.evidence: This is argued in the Appendix.

claims.claim: Many previous models postulated selective adaptation of competing representations to account for serial dependency.
claims.source: Many previous models of BR (e.g., Laing and Chow, 2002) postulated selective adaptation of competing representations to account for serial dependency.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous model.

claims.claim: Selective adaptation is an opponent process that favors positive correlations between different dominance periods, but negative correlations between same dominance periods.
claims.source: However, selective adaptation is an opponent process that favors positive correlations between different dominance periods, but negative correlations between same dominance periods.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical analysis of adaptation-based models.

claims.claim: Many well-known features of BR are reproduced, and indeed guaranteed, by the proposed dynamical mechanism.
claims.source: We have shown that many well-known features of BR are reproduced, and indeed guaranteed, by a particular dynamical mechanism.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claims.claim: The mechanism reproduces the counterintuitive input dependence of dominance durations, the stereotypical shape of dominance distributions, and the positive sequential correlation of dominance periods.
claims.source: Specifically, this mechanism reproduces the counterintuitive input dependence of dominance durations ('Levelt's propositions'), the stereotypical shape of dominance distributions ('scaling property'), and the positive sequential correlation of dominance periods.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claims.claim: The explanatory power of the proposed mechanism is considerably higher than that of previous models.
claims.source: The explanatory power of the proposed mechanism is considerably higher than that of previous models.
claims.evidence: This is argued based on the comprehensive reproduction of experimental observations.

claims.claim: The observations explained exhibited more effective degrees of freedom (approximately 14) than the mechanism itself (between 3 and 4).
claims.source: Indeed, the observations explained exhibited more effective degrees of freedom (approximately 14) than the mechanism itself (between 3 and 4).
claims.evidence: This is based on the analysis of the fitting procedure.

claims.claim: The proposed mechanism is biophysically plausible in terms of the out-of-equilibrium dynamics of a modular and hierarchical network of spiking neurons.
claims.source: The proposed mechanism is biophysically plausible in terms of the out-of-equilibrium dynamics of a modular and hierarchical network of spiking neurons (see also further below).
claims.evidence: This is argued based on the spiking network implementation.

claims.claim: Individual modules idealize the input dependence of attractor transitions in assemblies of spiking neurons.
claims.source: Individual modules idealize the input dependence of attractor transitions in assemblies of spiking neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model architecture.

claims.claim: All synaptic effects superimpose linearly, consistent with extended mean-field theory for neuronal networks.
claims.source: All synaptic effects superimpose linearly, consistent with extended mean-field theory for neuronal networks (Amit and Brunel, 1997; Van Vreeswijk and Sompolinski, 1996).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claims.claim: The interaction between 'rivaling' sets of modules results in divisive normalization, which is consistent with many cortical models.
claims.source: The interaction between 'rivaling' sets of modules ('pools') results in divisive normalization, which is consistent with many cortical models (Carandini and Heeger, 2011; Miller, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: It has long been suspected that multistable phenomena in visual, auditory, and tactile perception may share a similar mechanistic origin.
claims.source: It has long been suspected that multistable phenomena in visual, auditory, and tactile perception may share a similar mechanistic origin.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: Similar out-of-equilibrium dynamics of modular networks may underlie all multistable phenomena in all sensory modalities.
claims.source: As the features of BR explained here are in fact universal features of multistable phenomena in different modalities, we hypothesize that similar out-of-equilibrium dynamics of modular networks may underlie all multistable phenomena in all sensory modalities.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the findings of the manuscript.

claims.claim: This may be a general mechanism operating in many perceptual representations.
claims.source: In other words, we hypothesize that this may be a general mechanism operating in many perceptual representations.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the findings of the manuscript.

claims.claim: Two principal alternatives have been considered for the dynamical mechanism of perceptual decision-making: drift-diffusion models and recurrent network models.
claims.source: Two principal alternatives have been considered for the dynamical mechanism of perceptual decision-making: drift-diffusion models (Luce, 1986; Ratcliff and Smith, 2004) and recurrent network models (Wang, 2008; Wang, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The mechanism proposed here combines both alternatives: at its evidence level, sensory information is integrated by 'local attractors' in a discrete version of a drift-diffusion process, and at its decision level, the population dynamics of a recurrent network implements a winner-take-all competition between 'non-local attractors'.
claims.source: The mechanism proposed here combines both alternatives: at its evidence level, sensory information is integrated, over both space and time, by 'local attractors' in a discrete version of a drift-diffusion process. At its decision level, the population dynamics of a recurrent network implements a winner-take-all competition between 'non-local attractors.'
claims.evidence: This is a description of the proposed mechanism.

claims.claim: Together, the two levels form a 'nested attractor' system operating perpetually out of equilibrium.
claims.source: Together, the two levels form a 'nested attractor' system (Braun and Mattia, 2010) operating perpetually out of equilibrium.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the proposed mechanism with a citation.

claims.claim: A recurrent network with strong competition typically 'normalizes' individual responses relative to the total response.
claims.source: A recurrent network with strong competition typically 'normalizes' individual responses relative to the total response (Miller, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Divisive normalization is considered a canonical cortical computation.
claims.source: Divisive normalization is considered a canonical cortical computation (Carandini and Heeger, 2011), for which multiple rationales can be found.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Divisive normalization is augmented by indiscriminate feedforward inhibition in the proposed mechanism.
claims.source: Here, divisive normalization is augmented by indiscriminate feedforward inhibition.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the proposed mechanism.

claims.claim: The combination of divisive normalization and indiscriminate feedforward inhibition ensures that decision activity rapidly and reliably categorizes differential input strength, largely independently of total input strength.
claims.source: This combination ensures that decision activity rapidly and reliably categorizes differential input strength, largely independently of total input strength.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model properties.

claims.claim: Selective suppression of evidence for a winning hypothesis features in computational theories of 'hierarchical inference'.
claims.source: Selective suppression of evidence for a winning hypothesis features in computational theories of 'hierarchical inference' (Rao and Ballard, 1999; Lee and Mumford, 2003; Parr and Friston, 2017b; Pezzulo et al., 2018), as well as in accounts of multistable perception inspired by such theories (Dayan, 1998; Hohwy et al., 2008; Weilnhammer et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claims.claim: A normative reason for feedback suppression arises during continuous inference in uncertain and volatile environments, where optimal change detection requires an exponentially rising bias against evidence for the most likely state.
claims.source: A normative reason for feedback suppression arises during continuous inference in uncertain and volatile environments, where the accumulation of sensory information is ongoing and cannot be restricted to appropriate intervals (Veliz-Cuba et al., 2016). Here, optimal change detection requires an exponentially rising bias against evidence for the most likely state, ensuring that even weak changes are detected, albeit with some delay.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to work on optimal inference.

claims.claim: The pivotal feature of the proposed mechanism are pools of bistable variables or 'local attractors'.
claims.source: The pivotal feature of the proposed mechanism are pools of bistable variables or 'local attractors.'
claims.evidence: This is a description of the proposed mechanism.

claims.claim: Encoding sensory inputs in terms of persistent 'activations' of local attractors creates an intrinsically retentive representation: sites that respond are also sites that retain information (for a limited time).
claims.source: Encoding sensory inputs in terms of persistent 'activations' of local attractors assemblies (rather than in terms of transient neuronal spikes) creates an intrinsically retentive representation: sites that respond are also sites that retain information (for a limited time).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model properties.

claims.claim: The results are consistent with a few tens of bistable variables in each pool.
claims.source: Our results are consistent with a few tens of bistable variables in each pool.
claims.evidence: This is based on the model fitting results.

claims.claim: In the proposed mechanism, differential activity of two pools accumulates evidence against the dominant appearance until a threshold is reached and a reversal ensues.
claims.source: In the proposed mechanism, differential activity of two pools accumulates evidence against the dominant appearance until a threshold is reached and a reversal ensues (see also Barniv and Nelken, 2015; Nguyen et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model mechanism with citations to similar models.

claims.claim: This discrete non-equilibrium dynamics might instantiate a variational principle of inference such as 'maximum caliber'.
claims.source: Conceivably, this discrete non-equilibrium dynamics might instantiate a variational principle of inference such as 'maximum caliber' (Pressé et al., 2013; Dixit et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative suggestion with citations.

claims.claim: The components of the proposed mechanism interact to guarantee the statistical features that characterize BR and other multistable phenomena.
claims.source: The components of the proposed mechanism interact to guarantee the statistical features that characterize BR and other multistable phenomena.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claims.claim: Discretely stochastic accumulation of differential evidence against the dominant appearance ensures sensitivity of dominance durations to non-dominant input.
claims.source: Discretely stochastic accumulation of differential evidence against the dominant appearance ensures sensitivity of dominance durations to non-dominant input.
claims.evidence: This is a description of how the model reproduces Levelt II.

claims.claim: Discretely stochastic accumulation ensures the invariance of relative variability ('scaling property') and gamma-like distribution shape of dominance durations.
claims.source: It also ensures the invariance of relative variability ('scaling property') and gamma-like distribution shape of dominance durations.
claims.evidence: This is a description of how the model reproduces the scaling property.

claims.claim: Due to a non-trivial interaction with the competitive decision, discretely stochastic fluctuations of evidence-level activity express themselves in a serial dependency of dominance durations.
claims.source: Due to a non-trivial interaction with the competitive decision, discretely stochastic fluctuations of evidence-level activity express themselves in a serial dependency of dominance durations.
claims.evidence: This is a description of how the model reproduces serial dependencies.

claims.claim: Several features of serial dependency were unexpected and not reported previously, for example, the sensitivity to image contrast and the 'burstiness' of dominance reversals.
claims.source: Several features of this dependency were unexpected and not reported previously, for example, the sensitivity to image contrast and the 'burstiness' of dominance reversals (i.e., extended episodes in which dominance periods are consistently longer or shorter than average).
claims.evidence: This is a description of novel predictions.

claims.claim: The fact that these predictions are confirmed by experimental observations provides further support for the proposed mechanism.
claims.source: The fact that these predictions are confirmed by our experimental observations provides further support for the proposed mechanism.
claims.evidence: This is based on the experimental confirmation of model predictions.

claims.claim: The proposed mechanism is of similar complexity as previous minimal models in that it assumes four state variables at two dynamical levels, one slow (accumulation) and one fast (winner-take-all competition).
claims.source: How does the proposed mechanism compare to previous 'dynamical' models of multistable phenomena? It is of similar complexity as previous minimal models (Laing and Chow, 2002; Wilson, 2007; Moreno-Bote et al., 2010) in that it assumes four state variables at two dynamical levels, one slow (accumulation) and one fast (winner-take-all competition).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with previous models.

claims.claim: The proposed mechanism differs from previous models in reversing the ordering of slow and fast levels: visual input impinges first on the slow level, which then drives the fast level.
claims.source: It differs in reversing their ordering: visual input impinges first on the slow level, which then drives the fast level.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with previous models.

claims.claim: The proposed mechanism differs from previous models in that stochasticity dominates the slow dynamics, not the fast dynamics.
claims.source: It also differs in that stochasticity dominates the slow dynamics (as suggested by van Ee, 2009), not the fast dynamics.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with previous models with a citation.

claims.claim: The most fundamental difference from previous models is discreteness (pools of bistable variables), which shapes all key dynamical properties.
claims.source: However, the most fundamental difference is discreteness (pools of bistable variables), which shapes all key dynamical properties.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with previous models.

claims.claim: Unlike many previous models, the proposed mechanism does not include adaptation (stimulation-driven weakening of evidence), but a phenomenologically similar feedback suppression (perception-driven weakening of evidence).
claims.source: Unlike many previous models (e.g., Laing and Chow, 2002; Wilson, 2007; Moreno-Bote et al., 2007; Moreno-Bote et al., 2010; Cohen et al., 2019), the proposed mechanism does not include adaptation (stimulation-driven weakening of evidence), but a phenomenologically similar feedback suppression (perception-driven weakening of evidence).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with previous models.

claims.claim: Evidence from perceptual aftereffects supports the existence of both stimulation- and perception-driven adaptation, albeit at different levels of representation.
claims.source: Evidence from perceptual aftereffects supports the existence of both stimulation- and perception-driven adaptation, albeit at different levels of representation.
claims.evidence: This is based on empirical evidence.

claims.claim: Aftereffects in the perception of simple visual features are driven by stimulation rather than by perceived dominance.
claims.source: Aftereffects in the perception of simple visual features – such as orientation, spatial frequency, or direction of motion (Blake and Fox, 1974; Lehmkuhle and Fox, 1975; Wade and Wenderoth, 1978) – are driven by stimulation rather than by perceived dominance, whereas aftereffects in complex features – such as spiral motion, subjective contours, rotation in depth (Wiesenfelder and Blake, 1990; Van der Zwan and Wenderoth, 1994; Pastukhov et al., 2014a) – typically depend on perceived dominance.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claims.claim: Several experimental observations related to BR have been attributed to stimulation-driven adaptation.
claims.source: Several experimental observations related to BR have been attributed to stimulation-driven adaptation (e.g., negative priming, flash suppression, generalized flash suppression; Tsuchiya et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to empirical work.

claims.claim: The extent to which a perception-driven adaptation could also explain these observations remains an open question for future work.
claims.source: The extent to which a perception-driven adaptation could also explain these observations remains an open question for future work.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claims.claim: Multistable perception induces a positive priming or 'sensory memory', which can stabilize a dominant appearance during intermittent presentation.
claims.source: Multistable perception induces a positive priming or 'sensory memory' (Pearson and Clifford, 2005; Pastukhov and Braun, 2008; Pastukhov et al., 2013a), which can stabilize a dominant appearance during intermittent presentation (Leopold et al., 2003; Maier et al., 2003; Sandberg et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claims.claim: Positive priming exhibits rather different characteristics than the negative priming/adaptation of rivaling representations.
claims.source: This positive priming exhibits rather different characteristics (e.g., shape-, size- and motion-specificity, inducement period, persistence period) than the negative priming/adaptation of rivaling representations (de Jong et al., 2012; Pastukhov et al., 2013a; Pastukhov and Braun, 2013b; Pastukhov et al., 2014a; Pastukhov et al., 2014b; Pastukhov, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claims.claim: Sensory memory is mediated by additional levels of representation and not by self-stabilization of rivaling representations.
claims.source: To our mind, this evidence suggest that sensory memory is mediated by additional levels of representation and not by self-stabilization of rivaling representations, as has been suggested (Noest et al., 2007; Leptourgos, 2020).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of empirical evidence with citations.

claims.claim: To incorporate sensory memory, the present model would have to be extended to include three hierarchical levels (evidence, decision, and memory).
claims.source: To incorporate sensory memory, the present model would have to be extended to include three hierarchical levels (evidence, decision, and memory), as previously proposed by Gigante et al., 2009.
claims.evidence: This is a suggestion for future work with a citation.

claims.claim: No rivalry ensues when the stimulated locations in the left and right eye are more distant from each other.
claims.source: No rivalry ensues when the stimulated locations in the left and right eye are more distant from each other.
claims.evidence: This is based on empirical knowledge.

claims.claim: The computational model presented here encompasses only one local region, and therefore cannot reproduce spatially extended phenomena such as piecemeal rivalry or traveling waves.
claims.source: The computational model presented here encompasses only one such local region, and therefore cannot reproduce spatially extended phenomena such as piecemeal rivalry (Blake et al., 1992) or traveling waves (Wilson et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is a limitation of the model with citations.

claims.claim: To account for spatially extended phenomena, the visual field would have to be tiled with replicant models linked by grouping interactions.
claims.source: To account for these phenomena, the visual field would have to be tiled with replicant models linked by grouping interactions (Knapen et al., 2007; Bressloff and Webber, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is a suggestion for future work with citations.

claims.claim: A previous model postulated a hierarchy with competing and adapting representations at two separate levels, one lower (monocular) and another higher (binocular) level.
claims.source: A particularly intriguing previous model (Wilson, 2003) postulated a hierarchy with competing and adapting representations in eight state variables at two separate levels, one lower (monocular) and another higher (binocular) level.
claims.evidence: This is a description of a previous model with a citation.

claims.claim: The hierarchical model presented here could also account for this phenomenon if it were to be replicated at two successive levels.
claims.source: We expect that our hierarchical model could also account for this phenomenon if it were to be replicated at two successive levels.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the model's capabilities.

claims.claim: Such 'stacking' might have a normative justification in that it might subserve hierarchical inference.
claims.source: It is tempting to speculate that such 'stacking' might have a normative justification in that it might subserve hierarchical inference (Yuille and Kersten, 2006; Hohwy et al., 2008; Friston, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation with citations.

claims.claim: Another previous model used a hierarchy with 24 state variables at three separate levels to show that a stabilizing influence of selective visual attention could also explain slow rivalry when images are swapped rapidly.
claims.source: Another previous model (Li et al., 2017) used a hierarchy with 24 state variables at three separate levels to show that a stabilizing influence of selective visual attention could also explain slow rivalry when images are swapped rapidly.
claims.evidence: This is a description of a previous model with a citation.

claims.claim: The complex model by Li et al. reproduced the main features of Levelt's propositions, but did not consider scaling property and sequential dependency.
claims.source: Additionally, this rather complex model reproduced the main features of Levelt's propositions, but did not consider scaling property and sequential dependency.
claims.evidence: This is a description of a previous model.

claims.claim: The model by Li et al. shared some of the key features of the present model (divisive inhibition, differential excitation-inhibition), but added a multiplicative attentional modulation.
claims.source: The model shared some of the key features of the present model (divisive inhibition, differential excitation-inhibition), but added a multiplicative attentional modulation.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with a previous model.

claims.claim: As the present model already incorporates the 'biased competition' that is widely thought to underlie selective attention, it could reproduce attentional effects by means of additive modulations.
claims.source: As the present model already incorporates the 'biased competition' that is widely thought to underlie selective attention (Sabine and Ungerleider, 2000; Reynolds and Heeger, 2009), we expect that it could reproduce attentional effects by means of additive modulations.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the model's capabilities with citations.

claims.claim: The notion that multistable phenomena such as BR reflect active exploration of explanatory hypotheses for sensory evidence has a venerable history.
claims.source: The notion that multistable phenomena such as BR reflect active exploration of explanatory hypotheses for sensory evidence has a venerable history (von Helmholtz, 1867; Barlow et al., 1972; Gregory, 1980; Leopold and Logothetis, 1999).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to classic work.

claims.claim: The mechanism proposed here is in keeping with the notion that multistable phenomena reflect active exploration of explanatory hypotheses: higher-level 'explanations' compete for control of phenomenal appearance in terms of their correspondence to lower-level 'evidence'.
claims.source: The mechanism proposed here is in keeping with that notion: higher-level 'explanations' compete for control ('dominance') of phenomenal appearance in terms of their correspondence to lower-level 'evidence.'
claims.evidence: This is a description of the proposed mechanism.

claims.claim: An 'explanation' takes control if its correspondence is sufficiently superior to that of rival 'explanations'.
claims.source: An 'explanation' takes control if its correspondence is sufficiently superior to that of rival 'explanations.'
claims.evidence: This is a description of the proposed mechanism.

claims.claim: The greater the superiority, the longer control is retained.
claims.source: The greater the superiority, the longer control is retained.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the proposed mechanism.

claims.claim: Eventually, alternative 'explanations' seize control, if only briefly.
claims.source: Eventually, alternative 'explanations' seize control, if only briefly.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the proposed mechanism.

claims.claim: This manner of operation is consistent with computational theories of 'analysis by synthesis' or 'hierarchical inference', although there are many differences in detail.
claims.source: This manner of operation is also consistent with computational theories of 'analysis by synthesis' or 'hierarchical inference,' although there are many differences in detail (Rao and Ballard, 1999; Parr and Friston, 2017b; Pezzulo et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical frameworks.

claims.claim: Interacting with an uncertain and volatile world necessitates continuous and concurrent evaluation of sensory evidence and selection of motor action.
claims.source: Interacting with an uncertain and volatile world necessitates continuous and concurrent evaluation of sensory evidence and selection of motor action (Cisek and Kalaska, 2010; Gold and Stocker, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Multistable phenomena exemplify continuous decision-making without external prompting.
claims.source: Multistable phenomena exemplify continuous decision-making without external prompting (Braun and Mattia, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Sensory decision-making has been studied extensively, mostly in episodic choice-task, and the neural circuits and activity dynamics underlying episodic decision-making have been traced in detail.
claims.source: Sensory decision-making has been studied extensively, mostly in episodic choice-task, and the neural circuits and activity dynamics underlying episodic decision-making – including representations of potential choices, sensory evidence, and behavioral goals – have been traced in detail (Cisek and Kalaska, 2010; Gold and Shadlen, 2007; Wang, 2012; Krug, 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: There seems to be substantial overlap between choice representations in decision-making and in multistable situations.
claims.source: Interestingly, there seems to be substantial overlap between choice representations in decision-making and in multistable situations (Braun and Mattia, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Continuous inference has been studied extensively in auditory streaming paradigms.
claims.source: Continuous inference has been studied extensively in auditory streaming paradigms (Winkler et al., 2012; Denham et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The auditory system seems to continually update expectations for sound patterns on the basis of recent experience.
claims.source: The auditory system seems to continually update expectations for sound patterns on the basis of recent experience.
claims.evidence: This is based on empirical knowledge.

claims.claim: Compatible patterns are grouped together in auditory awareness, and incompatible patterns result in spontaneous reversals between alternatives.
claims.source: Compatible patterns are grouped together in auditory awareness, and incompatible patterns result in spontaneous reversals between alternatives.
claims.evidence: This is based on empirical knowledge.

claims.claim: Many aspects of auditory streaming phenomenology are reproduced by computational models driven by some kind of 'prediction error'.
claims.source: Many aspects of this rich phenomenology are reproduced by computational models driven by some kind of 'prediction error' (Mill et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The dynamics of two recent auditory models are rather similar to the model presented here: while one sound pattern dominates awareness, evidence against this pattern is accumulated at a subliminal level.
claims.source: The dynamics of two recent auditory models (Barniv and Nelken, 2015; Nguyen et al., 2020) are rather similar to the model presented here: while one sound pattern dominates awareness, evidence against this pattern is accumulated at a subliminal level.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with previous models with citations.

claims.claim: Ongoing activity in sensory cortex appears to be low-dimensional, in the sense that the activity of neurons with similar response properties varies concomitantly ('shared variability', 'noise correlations').
claims.source: Ongoing activity in sensory cortex appears to be low-dimensional, in the sense that the activity of neurons with similar response properties varies concomitantly ('shared variability,' 'noise correlations,' Ponce-Alvarez et al., 2012, Mazzucato et al., 2015, Engel et al., 2016, Rich and Wallis, 2016, Mazzucato et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claims.claim: Possible dynamical origins of shared and moderately slow variability have been studied extensively in theory and simulation.
claims.source: Possible dynamical origins of shared and moderately slow variability have been studied extensively in theory and simulation (for reviews, see Miller, 2016; Huang and Doiron, 2017; La Camera et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claims.claim: Networks with weakly clustered connectivity can express a metastable attractor dynamics with moderately long time scales.
claims.source: Networks with weakly clustered connectivity (e.g., 3% rewiring) can express a metastable attractor dynamics with moderately long time scales (Litwin-Kumar and Doiron, 2012; Doiron and Litwin-Kumar, 2014; Schaub et al., 2015; Rosenbaum et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claims.claim: In a metastable dynamics, individual (connectivity-defined) clusters transition spontaneously between distinct and quasi-stationary activity levels ('attractor states').
claims.source: In a metastable dynamics, individual (connectivity-defined) clusters transition spontaneously between distinct and quasi-stationary activity levels ('attractor states') (Tsuda, 2001; Stern et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claims.claim: Evidence for metastable attractor dynamics in cortical activity is accumulating steadily.
claims.source: Evidence for metastable attractor dynamics in cortical activity is accumulating steadily (Mattia et al., 2013; Mazzucato et al., 2015; Rich and Wallis, 2016; Engel et al., 2016; Marcos et al., 2019; Mazzucato et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claims.claim: Distinct activity states with exponentially distributed durations have been reported in sensory cortex, consistent with noise-driven escape transitions.
claims.source: Distinct activity states with exponentially distributed durations have been reported in sensory cortex (Mazzucato et al., 2015; Engel et al., 2016), consistent with noise-driven escape transitions (Doiron and Litwin-Kumar, 2014; Huang and Doiron, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical and theoretical studies.

claims.claim: Several reports are consistent with external input modulating cortical activity mostly indirectly, via the rate of state transitions.
claims.source: And several reports are consistent with external input modulating cortical activity mostly indirectly, via the rate of state transitions (Fiser et al., 2004; Churchland et al., 2010; Mazzucato et al., 2015; Engel et al., 2016; Mazzucato et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claims.claim: The proposed mechanism assumes bistable variables with noise-driven escape transitions, with transition rates modulated exponentially by external synaptic drive.
claims.source: The proposed mechanism assumes bistable variables with noise-driven escape transitions, with transition rates modulated exponentially by external synaptic drive.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the proposed mechanism.

claims.claim: This is an accurate reduction of the population dynamics of metastable networks of spiking neurons.
claims.source: Following previous work (Cao et al., 2016), we show this to be an accurate reduction of the population dynamics of metastable networks of spiking neurons.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The spatial structure of the 'shared variability' or 'noise correlations' in cortical activity is poorly understood.
claims.source: Unfortunately, the spatial structure of the 'shared variability' or 'noise correlations' in cortical activity described above is poorly understood.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claims.claim: In each of V1 and V4, the neural representation of rivaling stimulation can comfortably accommodate several thousand recurrent local assemblies, each capable of expressing independent collective dynamics.
claims.source: Accordingly, in each of these two cortical areas, the neural representation of rivaling stimulation can comfortably accommodate several thousand recurrent local assemblies, each capable of expressing independent collective dynamics (i.e., 'classic columns' comprising several 'minicolumns' with distinct stimulus selectivity Nieuwenhuys R, 1994, Kaas, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The model assumes that the representation of two rivaling images engages approximately 1–2% of the available number of recurrent local assemblies.
claims.source: Thus, our model assumes that the representation of two rivaling images engages approximately 1–2% of the available number of recurrent local assemblies.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model assumptions.

claims.claim: Neurophysiological correlates of BR have been studied extensively, often by comparing reversals of phenomenal appearance during binocular stimulation with physical alternation of monocular stimulation.
claims.source: Neurophysiological correlates of BR have been studied extensively, often by comparing reversals of phenomenal appearance during binocular stimulation with physical alternation (PA) of monocular stimulation (e.g., Leopold and Logothetis, 1996; Scheinberg and Logothetis, 1997; Logothetis, 1998; Wilke et al., 2006; Aura et al., 2008; Keliris et al., 2010; Panagiotaropoulos et al., 2012; Bahmani et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2016; Kapoor et al., 2020; Dwarakanath et al., 2020).

claims.claim: In primary visual cortex (area V1), neurophysiological correlates of BR and PA diverge: modulation of spiking activity is weaker during BR than PA, whereas measures thought to record dendritic inputs are modulated comparably under both conditions.
claims.source: In primary visual cortex (area V1), where many neurons are dominated by input from one eye, neurophysiological correlates of BR and PA diverge in an interesting way: whereas modulation of spiking activity is weaker during BR than PA (Leopold and Logothetis, 1996; Logothetis, 1998; Wilke et al., 2006; Aura et al., 2008; Keliris et al., 2010), measures thought to record dendritic inputs are modulated comparably under both conditions (Aura et al., 2008; Keliris et al., 2010; Bahmani et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claims.claim: At an intermediate cortical level (visual area V4), some units modulate their spiking activity comparably during BR and PA, while other units exhibit the opposite modulation during BR.
claims.source: A stronger divergence is observed at an intermediate cortical level (visual area V4), where neurons respond to both eyes. Whereas some units modulate their spiking activity comparably during BR and PA (i.e., increased activity when preferred stimulus becomes dominant), other units exhibit the opposite modulation during BR (i.e., reduced activity when preferred stimulus gains dominance) (Leopold and Logothetis, 1996; Logothetis, 1998; Wilke et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.
